Pricing Architecture for Services Firms

The Commercial SystemPart 4

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 10-minute read · Strategy

A pricing architecture is the set of rules that turns a firm's rate card into the fee it actually keeps: the fee model, the packages, the discount and exception rules, the scope change terms and the payment terms. Most services firms have a rate card and no architecture, so the realised price is set deal by deal. That matters because price is the strongest profit lever available. Marn and Rosiello's classic Harvard Business Review analysis found a 1% price improvement, with volume unchanged, lifted operating profit by 11.1%, against 3.3% for a 1% volume gain. Design the architecture once, measure the gap between list and pocket price, and record every exception so the rules can learn.

Part 3 of this series covered which segments to pursue. Pricing is the next Strategy decision, and in services firms it is usually the least designed. A rate card exists. Proposals are priced by the partner or founder who writes them. Discounts are agreed in the last week of a deal. Nobody can say, at year end, what the firm realised against what it quoted.

A pricing architecture fixes that without making every proposal identical. It sets the rules that most deals follow, the limits within which people can use judgment, and the route for exceptions.

Price is the largest lever, and the least managed

The case for designing price rests on how far price moves profit. Marn and Rosiello's 1992 analysis in Harvard Business Review, using average economics across 2,463 companies, found a 1% improvement in price, with no loss of volume, increased operating profit by 11.1%. The same 1% improvement in volume added about 3.3%, a 1% cut in variable cost about 7.8%, and a 1% cut in fixed cost about 2.3%. The figures are old and the mix of companies was industrial, but the arithmetic holds wherever margins are thin relative to revenue.

More recent work points the same way. McKinsey's 2026 analysis of 140 public distributors found a 1% price increase could lift EBITDA margin by more than 22%, and described a building materials distributor where sales staff were overriding system prices in more than half of all transactions until a pricing architecture cut manual overrides by 80%. Distributors are not services firms. The pattern, discretion without rules leaking margin, is the same.

What a pricing architecture contains

ElementThe question it answersWhat it looks like in a services firm
Value metricWhat the client pays forDays, deliverables, outcomes, a retained capacity, or a mix
Fee modelHow the fee is structuredProject, retainer, time and materials, success fee or hybrid
PackagesWhich standard offers existTwo to four defined scopes with a price each
Rate cardWhat a unit of time or work costsRates by role, used for estimating and change requests
Discount rulesWho may lower the price, by how much, and whyApproval levels and allowed reasons
Scope change termsWhat happens when work growsChange request threshold and pricing method
Payment termsWhen the money arrivesDeposit, milestones, days to pay, late-payment terms
Review rhythmWhen the rules are checked against resultsQuarterly comparison of quoted, invoiced and collected

Most firms have the rate card and some packages. The elements that protect realised price, discount rules, scope change terms and the review rhythm, are the ones usually missing.

Choosing the fee model

The fee model decides who carries risk and what behaviour the fee rewards. Our piece on how marketing services are priced makes the point that the clearest guide to a provider's incentive is what makes its fee go up (How marketing services are priced). The same test applies to a firm pricing its own work.

Fee modelWhat it rewardsWho carries estimation riskSuits
Time and materialsHours workedThe clientUnclear scope, short or exploratory work
Fixed project feeFinishing efficientlyThe firmDefined deliverables with a clear end
RetainerKeeping the relationshipShared; drifts to the firm if scope growsOngoing work with a stable shape
Success or outcome feeThe agreed outcomeThe firmMeasurable outcomes the firm can influence
Hybrid: fixed base plus variableBoth delivery and outcomeSharedEngagements with a defined core and uncertain upside

Time-based pricing deserves particular scrutiny. It ties revenue directly to utilisation, and utilisation is under pressure. SPI Research's 2026 Professional Services Maturity Benchmark, published with Deltek, put billable utilisation at 66.4%, its lowest in nearly two decades, against 75% for high-performing firms. Thomson Reuters' 2026 survey of more than 1,500 professionals recorded growing concern that AI may threaten billing models. If AI shortens the hours a task takes, a firm billing by the hour passes the whole gain to the client. A fixed fee or a value metric lets the firm keep part of it. Our piece on seats, usage and outcomes covers the same choice for software (Seats, usage or outcomes).

The pocket price: where services firms leak

Marn and Rosiello defined the pocket price as the revenue truly left in a company's pocket from a transaction, after every deduction between list and payment. They called the chart of those deductions the pocket price waterfall. Services firms have their own version.

Step (illustrative engagement)AmountRemaining
Work delivered at rate card: 500 hours at $200$100,000
Negotiated discount at contract, 10%−$10,000$90,000
Overrun absorbed without a change request: 40 hours−$8,000$82,000
Invoice written off after a dispute−$2,000$80,000
Cost of payment received 90 days late, at 8% a year−$1,600$78,400
Pocket price$78,400, or 78.4% of standard value

The discount is the line everyone sees. In this example it is less than half the leak. The overrun, the write-off and the slow payment are rarely reported together, because they sit with delivery, finance and the account lead respectively. A pricing architecture puts them on one page.

The discount is the leak everyone sees. In most services engagements it is less than half of the loss.

Discount and exception rules

Discounts are not wrong. Undesigned discounts are. Ebsta's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities, found discounts offered early in a deal were associated with a 39% drop in win rates. Early discounting tends to signal that the price was never firm.

A simple rule set covers most firms.

Discount or exceptionWho approvesRequired on the record
Up to 5%, standard termsThe deal ownerReason from an agreed list
5% to 15%, or a non-standard payment termCommercial leadReason, what the client gives in return, expected outcome
Above 15%, a cap on change requests, or a success-only feeFounder or finance leadFull rationale, risk to margin, review date
Any price for a segment the firm has declinedCommercial leadWhy the exception is worth taking

Two principles make the rules work. First, every discount should trade for something: a longer term, a faster decision, a case study, a larger scope or prepayment. A discount that buys nothing is a price cut. Second, the allowed reasons should come from a short, fixed list, so exceptions can be compared over a year.

Recording price decisions so the rules learn

A pricing architecture improves only if its exceptions are graded. That requires the record The Build Order describes: each exception with its reason, approver, status and expected outcome, written back when the outcome is known (The ten commercial decisions worth recording).

After two or three quarters the record answers questions that otherwise run on anecdote. Did discounted proposals win more often than standard ones in each segment? Which reasons predicted renewals? Which clients generated most absorbed overrun? In Part 10 of The Build Order, a composite distributor found its discounts won no more often than standard quotes in some product lines once the outcomes were recorded (The same build in four industries). Services firms usually find something similar.

Pricing for AI-assisted work adds a new question. Software vendors are moving to hybrid structures: Metronome's 2026 review of more than 50 AI pricing models, a vendor catalogue, found most combine subscriptions with usage or credits. Services firms delivering AI-assisted work face the same choice between charging for effort and charging for the result (What is outcome-based pricing for AI?). Whatever they choose, the record makes the effect visible.

Illustrative example: closing the overrun leak
Decision
Require a change request for any overrun above 10% of estimated hours, priced at the rate card, before the work is done.
Reason and owner
A quarterly comparison of quoted, invoiced and collected fees showed absorbed overruns cost more than negotiated discounts across the year. Owned by the head of delivery; agreed with the commercial lead.
What changed
Proposals state the change threshold; project leads log overruns weekly; the pricing review now reports discounts, overruns, write-offs and days to pay on one page.

Illustrative: a composite of a 120-person technical services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Design the rules, not every price. An architecture sets defaults, limits and an exception route.
  • Measure pocket price. Discounts, overruns, write-offs and slow payment belong on one page.
  • Choose the fee model by risk and reward. Hourly billing passes efficiency gains, including AI gains, to the client.
  • Make every discount trade for something. Record the reason and grade the outcome.
Gateway card

Before you call it a pricing architecture

  • A chosen fee model and value metric for each offer
  • Two to four packages with stated scope and price
  • Discount approval levels with a fixed list of allowed reasons
  • A change request threshold written into every proposal
  • A quarterly report of quoted, invoiced and collected fees
  • Every exception recorded with an approver and an expected outcome

Sources and notes

  • Marn and Rosiello, "Managing Price, Gaining Profit", Harvard Business Review, September to October 1992. Classic analysis using Compustat averages; industrial companies, older data.
  • McKinsey, Pricing in distribution: A strategic growth engine, July 2026. Distribution sector, not services; case figures are McKinsey's.
  • Deltek, Professional services billable utilisation at a historic low, October 2026, summarising SPI Research's 2026 benchmark. Vendor partner publication; sample not stated.
  • Thomson Reuters Institute, 2026 AI in Professional Services Report. Survey of 1,500+ professionals; attitudes rather than measured pricing change.
  • Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 B2B Sales Benchmarks. Vendor analysis of 4.2 million opportunities; association, not causation.
  • Metronome, 2026 trends from cataloguing 50+ AI pricing models, April 2026. Vendor catalogue; qualitative findings.
  • The waterfall, approval table and fee model table are lowob's illustration; figures are invented for the example.

Next move

Take your last ten completed engagements and build the waterfall for each: standard value, discount, absorbed overrun, write-offs and days to pay. The largest line is where your pricing architecture should start.
